posts.title: Sixty years on the quay: an open day at Pier 9
posts.excerpt: On Saturday 26 September the Pier 9 warehouse opens its gates to neighbours, families and former colleagues.
posts.content:
Tsumugi Trading was founded in 1964 by Martin Hale and Sumi Aoki as a two-desk office on the quay buying linen yarn. Sixty years later, we would like to show the people of Port Ellery where the work now happens. On Saturday 26 September the Pier 9 warehouse on Harbour Road is open from 10:00 to 15:00, and everyone is welcome.

Daniel Reyes, director of logistics, joined the company in 1994 as a forklift driver and now leads the warehouse and the customs team. He will take small groups along the loading bays at 10:30, 12:00 and 14:00, explaining how a container is booked in, checked against its packing list and stored until the buyer asks for it. Each tour lasts about forty minutes and starts at the gate house.

What the day includes

  • Warehouse tours at 10:30, 12:00 and 14:00
  • The sample light table and the quality corner
  • An archive photograph exhibition
  • Refreshments in the canteen

Visitors will be able to see the light table where the quality team photographs incoming samples, the solar roof that was added in 2015, and a small exhibition of photographs from the company archive, from the first yarn orders of the 1960s to the first container shipment in 1978. Margaret Hale, our chair, will be at the gate house in the afternoon to meet former colleagues.

Please wear flat, closed shoes. Forklifts stop moving while groups are in the bays, but the floor is still a working floor. Tea, coffee and sandwiches will be served in the canteen. Children are welcome when accompanied, and the site is step-free throughout.

No booking is needed. We look forward to seeing you on the quay.

posts.title: How we inspect a first order from a new factory
posts.excerpt: Every first order from a new factory is inspected in person. Here is what that means in practice.
posts.content:
Before Tsumugi Trading places a first order with a new partner factory, someone from the company visits it. This has been the rule since the early years, and Margaret Hale still follows it. We would rather lose a week in the calendar than discover a problem when the container is already at sea.

The visit in four steps

  • Walk the workshop and the stores
  • Review earlier orders and records
  • Sign a reference sample in writing
  • Return for a check before loading

The visit usually lasts two days. On the first day we walk through the workshop with the factory manager, look at how raw material is stored and handled, and talk with the supervisors about their working hours and their breaks. We ask to see the records for the last few orders, and we check the samples we received earlier against the production line.

On the second day we agree the specification in writing: the dimensions, the colours, the packing method and the tolerances that matter to the buyer. A sealed reference sample is signed by both sides and kept in the sample room at Quay Street. If the production later drifts away from that sample, we have something concrete to hold in our hands.

When the order is produced, a member of the quality team returns before loading. We check cartons at random against the packing list, photograph them on the light table and send the pictures to the buyer before the container leaves. If we find a fault, we say so, and the buyer decides whether to accept, rework or reject the batch.

This does not remove every risk. It does mean that the first order, the one with the most unknowns, is the one we look at most closely.

posts.title: Our packaging review, two years in
posts.excerpt: What we have changed in two years of looking at cartons, pallets and fillers, and what remains to be solved.
posts.content:
Two years ago, Ines Varga, our director of sustainability and sourcing, started a review of the packaging that moves through Pier 9. Every week, goods arrive in cartons, shrink wrap, wooden pallets and foam fillers, and a good part of it is thrown away within days. The review asked a simple question: which of these materials does the buyer really need?

What changed so far

  • Paper corners instead of foam on tableware
  • Woven tape instead of plastic strapping on textile pallets
  • Photographic damage records for every claim

The first result was modest. We asked partner factories to remove the extra inner bag from a range of tableware and to replace foam corners with moulded paper. For textiles, we replaced plastic strapping with woven tape on the pallets going to three of our regular buyers. None of these changes was dramatic, but together they reduced the weight of packaging per container.

The second result was more useful. By photographing damaged goods on the light table, the quality team could see which cartons really failed and which were over-protected. In several cases the thinner carton performed as well as the thicker one. In two cases it did not, and we went back to the original design.

There is still a long list of things we have not solved. Some buyers require retail-ready packaging that is hard to recycle. Some factories lack a local supplier of paper fillers. And we have no good answer yet for the shrink wrap used to hold pallets together on long sea routes.

We will keep reporting what we find, including the mistakes. If you are a buyer with views on packaging, or a factory with a better material, please write to the desk lead you work with and tell us what you have seen.

posts.title: Graduate programme 2027: applications open
posts.excerpt: Applications for the 2027 graduate programme are open until 30 November. Hanna Lind explains what a first year looks like.
posts.content:
Applications for the Tsumugi Trading graduate programme 2027 are now open. We are looking for six graduates who would like to learn how a trading company works from the inside, and who are happy to spend part of their first year on the warehouse floor as well as at a desk.

Who we are looking for

  • Graduates in any subject, with an interest in international trade
  • Good written English; other languages are welcome
  • Comfort with numbers and with careful, repeated checks

The programme lasts eighteen months and is run by Hanna Lind. In the first three months, every graduate follows a desk for a week at a time: textiles with Oliver Brandt, tableware with Clara Moretti and industrial materials with Yusuf Demir. You will listen to calls, read contracts, and learn how a quotation becomes an order.

The next three months are spent at Pier 9 with Daniel Reyes and the customs team. You will book in containers, check cartons against packing lists and learn why a single digit in a commodity code matters. Many people tell us afterwards that this was the part that taught them the most.

After that, you join a desk as a junior member of the team with a named mentor, and you take part in at least one factory visit with a senior colleague. You are not expected to know the trade already. You are expected to be curious, careful with details and willing to ask when you are unsure.

To apply, send a short letter and your CV to hello@tsumugi-trading.example by 30 November. We read every letter and answer every applicant. Interviews will be held at Quay Street in January, and the programme starts in September 2027.

posts.title: Consolidating shipments: fewer half-empty containers
posts.excerpt: How the logistics team now combines smaller orders into fuller containers, and what buyers need to plan for.
posts.content:
A container that leaves a factory half empty costs nearly as much to ship as a full one. For several years, our logistics team has been looking for ways to fill containers better, and this spring we changed the way small orders are planned.

What buyers can do

  • Share your delivery calendar early
  • Tell us which orders are flexible
  • Accept a small wait for a lower freight cost

Until now, each buyer order was shipped as soon as it was ready. Small orders often left in a half-empty container, and a second small order from a nearby factory followed a week later. Now the desk leads and the warehouse agree a weekly loading plan, and orders from factories in the same region are combined when the delivery dates allow it.

The change needs some patience from buyers. An order may wait a few days at the factory or at Pier 9 until the container is full. In return, the freight cost per carton falls, and fewer containers make the journey. When a delivery date is fixed and cannot move, we still ship at once and tell the buyer why.

Daniel Reyes and his team keep a simple record of every container: how full it was, how long the goods waited and whether the buyer was affected. After three months, the average container left with more cartons and the waiting time was within the limits we had agreed with the desks.

We will keep refining the plan. If you buy from us regularly, please tell your desk lead which of your orders can wait and which cannot. The more we know about your calendar, the better we can combine the shipments.

posts.title: A visit to our linen partner mill
posts.excerpt: Linen yarn was our first cargo in 1964. In March, Margaret Hale and Oliver Brandt returned to the mill that still spins it.
posts.content:
In March, Margaret Hale and Oliver Brandt of the textile desk travelled to the mill that supplied Tsumugi Trading with its first linen yarn in 1964. The mill has changed hands twice since then and is now run by the granddaughter of the original owner. The relationship has lasted through all of it.

What we looked at

  • The old and new spinning lines
  • Storage of raw flax and finished yarn
  • Shift patterns and rest breaks
  • Samples for the light table

The visit had a practical purpose. The mill is installing a new spinning line, and we wanted to see how the change would affect delivery dates and the quality of the yarn. The manager showed us the old and the new machines side by side, and we took away samples from both to test on the light table at Quay Street.

We also spent a morning with the supervisors, talking about shift patterns, rest breaks and the way temporary staff are hired in the busy season. These conversations are part of every factory visit. They take time, but they tell us more about a partner than a certificate on the wall.

Lunch was the same soup that Martin Hale is said to have eaten on his first visit, and the mill keeps a framed order slip from 1964 in the meeting room. Margaret Hale was shown the signature of her father, and the manager asked for a copy of the photograph we keep in our archive.

The new line will start production in the summer. The first yarn from it will go to the textile desk for testing before any customer order is placed on it. We will report on the results later in the year.
